title: 39 State Banking Groups Form BankChain Alliance for 2027 Blockchain Launch
dek: Thirty-nine U.S. state bankers associations have formed BankChain Alliance to build a common blockchain network for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, and automated settlement, targeting a 2027 launch. The member associations represent 3,283 banks with $21.8 trillion in assets, but individual bank commitments remain unspecified.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: 39 state banking associations representing $21.8 trillion in assets have announced BankChain Alliance, targeting 2027 launch for a bank-owned blockchain network for tokenized deposits and payments.
bottom_line: Watch for BankChain's technology partner announcement and the governance structure it selects; those decisions will signal whether the alliance can convert association-level backing into operational bank participation. The 2027 launch date will be invalidated if the technology selection slips beyond Q4 2026 or if the alliance's governance model fails to reach consensus on critical protocol decisions before launch.
body: Thirty-nine U.S. state bankers associations have formed BankChain Alliance to build a common blockchain network for tokenized deposits, stablecoins, smart payments and automated settlement, according to The Defiant. The alliance is targeting a 2027 launch but is not yet an operating payments network.

The member associations represent 3,283 banks with $21.8 trillion in assets, based on Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. call-report data as of March 31. The roster covers associations in Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming.

The alliance's Aug. 25 announcement said it is still selecting a technology partner and plans to make the network interoperable with other systems while inviting banks across the country to become owners. The alliance's website lists a board chaired by Kathy Kraninger, president and CEO of the Florida Bankers Association. Other directors include leaders of the Ohio, Nebraska, Texas, North Carolina, Missouri, Utah, New Hampshire and Massachusetts banking groups, as well as TekFactor founder Kim Askwith.

A critical caveat appears on the alliance's website: the associations are the participants, but their member banks have not individually committed to or joined the network unless separately indicated. Neither the announcement nor the alliance website specifies committed capital, member contributions or pricing. On funding, the alliance says it will invite banks nationwide to become owners, while American Banker reported that the group wants an ownership stake in the technology partner it selects. The project has completed the first phase of its request for proposals, Kraninger told American Banker. Compliance carried more weight than any other factor in the RFP, according to Corey LeBlanc, co-founder and chief technology officer of Locality Bank. Howard Headlee, president and CEO of the Utah Bankers Association, framed governance as the differentiator, saying BankChain is intended to give member banks "equal access to a network they own, where their voice is heard."

BankChain enters a field that already includes a competing bank-led initiative. The Clearing House, owned by 25 of the country's largest financial institutions and already clearing and settling more than $2 trillion each day through its existing networks, unveiled a tokenized-deposit initiative in June. That initiative is designed to clear and settle tokenized commercial-bank money onchain and connect blockchain activity with the RTP and CHIPS payment networks. The Clearing House's announcement did not give an operational launch date. BankChain has a broader stated product menu, including stablecoins and automated settlement, and a governance pitch built around state associations and banks of different sizes. BankChain is at an earlier stage than The Clearing House initiative: it must choose a technology provider and convert association-level sponsorship into commitments from individual banks before its 2027 target can be tested.
